title: Optimistic concurrency (RowVersion, 409 Conflict)
hook: Two users edit the same order at once — last write wins silently unless you add a concurrency token. RowVersion detects conflicts and lets your API return 409 Conflict instead of corrupting data.

blocks.text: Optimistic concurrency assumes conflicts are rare — reads do not lock rows; writes check that data has not changed since load. EF Core supports concurrency tokens: a property (often byte[] RowVersion or xmin in PostgreSQL) included in the WHERE clause of UPDATE. If zero rows match, DbUpdateConcurrencyException is thrown — another transaction modified the row first. Web APIs map this to HTTP 409 Conflict with Problem Details, letting the client refresh and retry. Pessimistic concurrency (SELECT FOR UPDATE) locks rows but hurts throughput — rarely used in stateless REST APIs.

entries.plainDefinition: Detect conflicts at save time rather than locking rows during read.
Auto-incrementing binary column SQL Server updates on every row change — ideal concurrency token.
Property marked [ConcurrencyCheck] or IsConcurrencyToken() in Fluent API.
HTTP status when update fails due to version mismatch — client should reload.

blocks.text: Without concurrency tokens, two PATCH requests can overwrite each other — lost updates in inventory, billing, or collaborative editing. Interviewers ask how EF detects conflicts, what HTTP status to return, and how clients should retry. RowVersion is SQL Server specific; PostgreSQL uses xmin via Npgsql; other databases use manual int Version column. Senior answer includes client contract: return current RowVersion in GET, require If-Match header or token in PUT body.

blocks.title: ETag correlation
blocks.body: RowVersion base64-encoded in an ETag header mirrors HTTP conditional requests — If-Match on PUT returns 412 Precondition Failed or map concurrency to 409 per your API standard.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Client loads resource
items.body: GET returns entity with RowVersion (in body or ETag header).

items.title: EF generates UPDATE
items.body: SQL includes AND RowVersion = @original in WHERE clause.

items.title: API responds 409
items.body: Problem Details explains conflict; client refreshes and retries merge.

snippet.label: Entity and Fluent API configuration
snippet.explanation: IsRowVersion() maps to SQL Server rowversion type — database auto-updates on change. Client never sets RowVersion; only sends back the value from GET.

snippet.label: Update endpoint with concurrency handling
snippet.explanation: Early check optional; SaveChanges is authoritative — EF compares original RowVersion in WHERE. DbUpdateConcurrencyException when another writer won the race. Return 409 per RFC 7807 Problem Details.

snippet.label: Manual int version for portable databases
snippet.explanation: Integer Version works on any database. Application or database trigger increments on update. Portable alternative when rowversion/xmin unavailable.

snippet.label: Diagnostics and client retry pattern
snippet.explanation: High 409 rate on same resource type signals design issue — optimistic may be wrong for inventory decrements. Monitor 409 as business metric, not just error.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: AsNoTracking load then Attach without original RowVersion — concurrency check skipped. Returning 500 on DbUpdateConcurrencyException — should be 409. Client never sends RowVersion — silent last-write-wins. Using optimistic concurrency for inventory stock decrement without additional constraints — use row-level lock or serialized transaction for hot counters.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: integration test with parallel PUT requests — exactly one succeeds, other gets 409. Application Insights custom metric for concurrency_conflict count. For hot rows (seat booking, inventory), optimistic alone may be insufficient — combine with CHECK constraint (Stock >= 0) or SERIALIZABLE isolation for decrement. RowVersion adds negligible storage; index not needed on token itself since it is in WHERE with primary key.

blocks.title: Concurrency strategy tradeoffs
rows: High conflict rate needs UX merge flow

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Not knowing EF adds concurrency token to WHERE clause. Returning 500 instead of 409. Saying pessimistic locking is 'always better' without throughput tradeoff. Unable to explain client retry/merge flow.

interviewTakeaways: Optimistic concurrency uses a token (RowVersion) in UPDATE WHERE — zero rows updated means conflict; map to HTTP 409.
When not enough: high-contention inventory or seat booking may need pessimistic lock or database constraint beyond RowVersion.
Production tip: return RowVersion in GET; log 409 rate; integration test parallel updates; CHECK constraints on invariants.

60s: RowVersion auto-updates on SQL Server. EF includes it in WHERE on SaveChanges. Conflict throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException — return 409 Problem Details. Client reloads, merges, retries with new token.
Follow-up: how does concurrency work with AsNoTracking and Attach updates?
commonPitfalls: DbUpdateConcurrencyException mapped to 500 — clients cannot distinguish conflict from server error.
Attach without original values — EF cannot generate correct WHERE, concurrency silently broken.

Strong answer: 'RowVersion on entities, IsRowVersion in Fluent API. GET returns token, PUT requires it. SaveChanges conflict → 409 with Problem Details. I monitor 409 rate and use CHECK constraints for invariants like stock >= 0.'
introducedIn: EF Core 1.0; ExecuteUpdate concurrency in EF Core 7+

jsTsCorrelations.note: Express/Fastify APIs often use ETag middleware for conditional PUT — semantically identical to EF RowVersion. Encode RowVersion as base64 ETag for standards-compliant clients.
TypeORM @VersionColumn() mirrors EF concurrency tokens — same lost-update problem and 409 response pattern in Node APIs.
